Ch1
Analyze the trade-off between model accuracy and energy efficiency in AI/ML pipelines. Using an example, explain how a data scientist can decide whether a marginal gain in accuracy justifies the additional computational and environmental cost.
 Examine the key stages of an AI/ML pipeline (data collection, training, inference, and deployment) and analyze which stage contributes most significantly to the overall carbon footprint. Justify your reasoning.
Analyze the relationship between large-scale computing infrastructure (e.g., data centers) and environmental impact. Break down the major factors responsible for high energy consumption in such systems.
Compare and analyze the energy consumption patterns during the training phase versus the inference phase of a machine learning model. Which phase poses a greater sustainability challenge in real-world deployment, and why?
A smart-city system uses data analytics for traffic prediction. Analyze how Green Data Science can help reduce energy consumption, fuel usage, and carbon emissions in such a system.’
A company has two machine learning models for an application. Model A provides 99% accuracy but requires significantly higher computational resources, while Model B provides 97% accuracy with much lower energy consumption. As a Green Data Scientist, analyze the accuracy–energy trade-off and recommend which model should be selected. Justify your answer based on sustainability and environmental impact.
Ch2
A soil moisture sensor collects data every second using the traditional fixed-interval method.
Using Adaptive Sampling, the sensor collects:
1 reading/minute for 18 hours during stable conditions 
1 reading/15 seconds for 4 hours during changing conditions 
4 readings/second for 2 hours during heavy rainfall 
Calculate:
a) Total number of readings collected using the traditional method.
b) Total number of readings collected using adaptive sampling.
c) Calculate the percentage reduction in the number of readings achieved through adaptive sampling.
A smart farm uses 500 IoT sensors to monitor soil moisture, temperature, and humidity. The sensors currently collect data at fixed intervals and transmit all readings to the cloud, resulting in high energy consumption and redundant data. Apply suitable sustainable data-acquisition techniques to redesign this system. Explain how your selected techniques reduce energy consumption while maintaining data quality. 
A wake-up radio system allows a node to remain in deep sleep (2 µW) and wake up only on receiving a trigger signal, with a wake-up latency of 15 ms and active power of 30 mW during processing. If the node receives an average of 10 trigger events per hour, each requiring 15 ms of active processing, calculate the total daily energy consumption and compare it with a node that stays continuously active at 30 mW.
A sensor node uses duty cycling with an active period of 200 ms and a sleep period of 1800 ms in each cycle. The active-mode power is 45 mW and sleep-mode power is 0.05 mW. Calculate:
(a) The duty cycle percentage.
(b) The average power consumption per cycle.
(c) The energy saved per hour compared to continuous active operation.
A wireless sensor node samples temperature data continuously at 1 sample/second, consuming 12 mA during active sensing and 0.5 mA in sleep mode, operating at 3.3V. If adaptive sampling reduces the active sampling rate to 1 sample every 10 seconds for stable conditions (assume 80% of the time is stable), calculate:
(a) The average current consumption before and after applying adaptive sampling.
(b) The percentage reduction in energy consumption over a 24-hour period.
An air-quality monitoring sensor records PM2.5 every second, resulting in a large number of unnecessary transmissions. Apply event-triggered sensing to design a mechanism that transmits data only when pollution levels cross a meaningful threshold. Explain how your approach reduces data and energy consumption.
Ch3
A mobile health-monitoring app uses a deep CNN for ECG anomaly detection, but the model is too large and slow for real-time inference on a smartwatch's limited battery. Apply structured pruning to propose which layers/channels you would prune and explain how this would improve performance-per-watt while maintaining diagnostic accuracy.
An edge-AI company wants to deploy an image classification model on a low-power IoT camera with limited memory and no dedicated GPU. Apply mixed-precision quantization techniques (e.g., converting FP32 weights to INT8/FP16 selectively) to design a deployment strategy, and justify which layers should retain higher precision.
A large language model (teacher) performs well for customer support chatbots but is too expensive to run at scale. Apply knowledge distillation to design a smaller student model deployment strategy, explaining how you would preserve response quality while significantly reducing inference cost and energy consumption.
A wildlife conservation project deploys battery-powered camera traps in remote forests to detect poachers using on-device AI, with no cloud connectivity. Apply TinyML and early-exit network concepts to design an inference pipeline that saves energy by exiting early on "easy" (clearly empty) frames while still processing complex frames fully.
A startup wants to fine-tune a large pre-trained vision-language model for a specific niche use case (e.g., agricultural pest identification) but has limited GPU budget for training. Apply Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) to propose a fine-tuning strategy, explaining how it reduces training cost and energy consumption compared to full fine-tuning.
